web_evidence.title: John Steinbeck: The Moon Is Down
web_evidence.note: Complete library scan shows sustained nonparticipating third-person narration throughout the opening, interior chapters, and conclusion, including access to multiple characters' thoughts; no first- or second-person base sections appear.

web_evidence.title: Cultural Trauma in John Steinbeck's The Moon Is Down
web_evidence.note: University-hosted scholarly thesis explicitly analyzes Steinbeck's third-person omniscient narrative technique across the novel.

web_evidence.title: The Moon Is Down LitChart
web_evidence.note: The guide explicitly identifies the work's point of view as third-person omniscient and analyzes scenes involving both occupiers and townspeople.

web_evidence.title: John Steinbeck Writing Styles in The Moon Is Down
web_evidence.note: The point-of-view section explicitly describes the novel as third-person omniscient, with access to the characters' thoughts and feelings.

web_evidence.title: John Steinbeck: Novels 1942–1952
web_evidence.note: Library of America confirms that the eligible work is a novel conceived alongside a play and told largely in dialogue; this explains the dialogue-heavy quote sample but is not itself person evidence.

search_log: Searched "John Steinbeck The Moon Is Down full text excerpt first chapter narration" and located a complete Internet Archive library scan plus chapter transcriptions.
Searched "The Moon Is Down John Steinbeck point of view third person narrator" and opened explicit whole-book descriptions from a university thesis, LitCharts, and BookRags.

person_note: The controlling narrator is nonparticipating and third-person omniscient, moving among characters on both sides of the occupation and reporting private beliefs or perceptions. Quotes q00215, q00221, q00222, and q00224 independently corroborate that position. The apparent first person in q00209 is Colonel Lanser's speech with lost quotation boundaries, not a narrator; the many other I, we, and you forms are likewise dialogue or gnomic address. q00220 appears misbucketed as dialogue but is nondiagnostic narratorial description. Whole-book library and scholarly evidence reveals no sustained first- or second-person section, epistolary layer, or narrative frame. The main limitation is that many supplied quotes are dialogue, but the diagnostic narration and strong web evidence agree.
